title: Introduction: RL vs. Scaffolds for Small Coding Models
text: I'm Ude Sonowane. If you want to make a small model good at coding, the literature gives you two levers, reinforcement learning and the agent you wrap around it. The published numbers mix them together and one open model reports three different scores on the same benchmark. Here is the thing to look at. Deepswe preview is a 32 billion parameter open model trained with reinforcement learning. On SWE verified, it scores 42.2. It also scores 59. It also scores 71. Same model, same 500 problems, same week. Those are not three attempts at one measurement. They are three different measurements and only one of them is something you can ship.

title: Decoding DeepSWE's Multiple Benchmark Scores
text: Three questions for any coding agent score. One, one run or best of end because best of end is a different product. Two, which scaffold and how much context the harness is not neutral. Three, who picked the winner, a verifier you can actually run or an oracle that already knows the answer. The third one is where most of the inflation lies. First, what was actually done? The base is QN3-32B. The training is reinforcement learning only, no distillation from a stronger model, which matters because most open coding models are fine-tuned on traces from something bigger. The algorithm is a modified GRPO 4500 real software tasks with every repository that appears in the benchmark filtered out of training first. 64H100 6 days. title: 3 Questions for Evaluating Coding Agent Claims
text: Is one attempt which is what a user gets. 57.9 is best of eight. 59 is best of 16 with a verifier choosing between them. And 71 is also best of 16, but chosen by an oracle that already knows which patch passes. That last one is an upper bound on the method. It is not a result you can deploy. Question two, the scaffold. In the same table, the authors published Devstral small scores 46.6 on one attempt. That is four points above deepsw's 42.2 from a model 8 billion parameters smaller. The difference is not obviously the model. One runs on open hands, the other on R2E gym with a 64,000 token window and 100 steps. Change the harness and the number moves.

title: DeepSWE Training: 32B Model, GRPO & Zero Distillation
text: This is the part that breaks the usual reading. That comparison table has 10 rows and four different scaffolds in it and three different test time settings. Some rows are one attempt, some are best of eight. Ranking them top to bottom produces a leaderboard that does not exist. The authors are not hiding this. The scaffold is a column in their own table. Almost nobody quoting the 59 reads that column. There is a second road and it is worth the comparison. SWESmith generated 50,000 training tasks across 128 repositories and fine-tuned on expert trajectories rather than using reinforcement learning. Its model scores 40.2 on one attempt. Reinforcement learning scored 42.2 points apart. Meanwhile, turning on best of 16 moved the same model by nearly 17. The training method is not where the big number came from. scored one run or best

title: Pass@1 vs. Best-of-16 (Verifiers vs. Oracles)
text: Of n. Three of the four published numbers are best of n which scaffold four of them in one table. Who picked the winner? A verifier for 59 and Oracle for 71. So be excited that a 32 billion parameter open model trained with reinforcement learning and no distillation does real work on real repositories. Be skeptical of any single number quoted without its scaffold in its n. And if you do want the 59, budget for it. Best of 16 means 16 times the inference. Your turn. Next time a coding model posts a number, find three things before you believe it. The scaffold, the N, and who chose the winner. If the model card does not say, that is your answer. One model, three numbers.
